abstract: 1. Climate and environmental change are altering the seasonal dynamics of insects worldwide, yet long-term datasets remain scarce for mosquito vectors in temperate regions. Consequently, the environmental drivers and phenological responses of mosquito populations are still poorly resolved in northern Europe. 2. Here, we test whether the seasonal timing and abundance of a specialist coastal mosquito are jointly shaped by climatic and tidal drivers, and whether its activity period has extended over a 14-year monitoring record. 3. We analysed a 14-year dataset (2012-2025) of the salt marsh mosquito Aedes detritus - one of the most common saltmarsh mosquitoes in Europe - collected from four British coastal wetland sites. Weekly catch data from the full time series were used to assess long-term phenological trends, while generalised additive models were applied to site-month aggregated observations from the consistent four-site trapping period (2019-2025) to identify climatic and tidal drivers of abundance. 4. Across the full 14-year record, the late-season peak and the end of the activity period (the 90% activity week) shifted later by 0.52 and 0.76 weeks per year, respectively (equivalent to fitted shifts of approximately 7 and 10 weeks), with no corresponding advance in the spring onset. This delayed autumn activity was robust to sampling-window and moving-window controls. 5. Adult abundance showed a pronounced bimodal seasonal pattern, with a smaller peak in late spring and a larger peak in mid-autumn. After accounting for seasonal structure, rainfall at a one-month lag and tidal surge were both positively associated with mosquito abundance. The size of the spring peak was correlated with rainfall, but the size and timing of the autumn peak were not. 6. These findings provide evidence that the seasonal activity of a salt marsh mosquito is extending later into autumn. We show that its population dynamics reflects a combination of climatic and tidal drivers whose relative contributions will require longer or more finely resolved records to disentangle fully. Sustained, long-term, full-season monitoring of coastal mosquito populations would therefore be important for understanding their responses to climate change. We recommend extending mosquito sampling in salt marsh areas into late autumn to better assess future risks associated with mosquito-borne pathogens.
